title: Chest drain and needle aspiration in neonates
subject: paediatrics
summary: Drain a neonatal pneumothorax or effusion causing distress, low oxygen saturation or instability. Aspirate air through the 2nd or 3rd intercostal space in the midclavicular line, or place a 10 or 12 Fr drain in the 4th or 5th space between the anterior and midaxillary lines, inserted 2 to 3 cm in small preterm and 3 to 4 cm in term babies. Confirm on AP and lateral X-ray.

sections.title: Indications
items: Drain a pneumothorax causing respiratory distress, low oxygen saturation or haemodynamic instability. With mild distress and no severe instability, one surgical unit tried needle aspiration first and placed a tube only if air kept accumulating.
Drains also remove fluid: effusion, chylothorax, haemothorax and empyema.

sections.title: Needle aspiration
items: Attach a needle or angiocatheter to a 10 to 20 mL syringe and enter the 2nd or 3rd intercostal space in the midclavicular line. Stop advancing as soon as air flows into the syringe, to avoid lung injury.
Alternative site: 4th to 5th intercostal space in the midaxillary line, needle pointed toward the opposite shoulder. Ultrasound guidance can be used instead of fixed landmarks.
Systematic reviews found no difference between needle aspiration and chest tube in safety or immediate success; aspiration causes less pain and a shorter hospital stay.

sections.title: Chest drain
items: Site (Buelau position): between the anterior and midaxillary lines in the 4th or 5th intercostal space, just above the rib margin; safe on both sides in preterm and term babies.
Drain size 10 or 12 Fr. Insertion length 2 to 3 cm in small preterm and 3 to 4 cm in term infants.
For air, aim the tip anteriorly: enter near the anterior axillary line and direct the tip toward the xiphisternum, away from breast tissue. For fluid, place the tip posterior to the lung.

Pigtail catheters (Seldinger) and traditional tubes have comparable safety and effectiveness; pigtails are fast and easy in preterm babies. Trocar insertion needs more force and is linked to more organ injury.
Point-of-care ultrasound guidance gives high success and few complications.

sections.title: After insertion
items: Get AP and lateral chest X-rays immediately. The tip and all side holes must lie in the pleural space.
For a persistent air leak after drainage, one unit used continuous suction at 5 to 10 cmH2O and advised against a second or third drain.

sections.title: Complications and pitfalls
items: Minor: dislodgement and blockage. Major: infection, lung laceration or perforation, effusion, pericardial perforation, phrenic nerve injury and diaphragm paralysis.
In preterm babies the pericardium is close to the skin entry point: a drain advanced on its mandrel perforated the pericardium and caused tamponade. Plan the path and depth, and use ultrasound.
Subcutaneous emphysema has followed trocar drain placement; the reporting unit switched to Seldinger pigtail catheters.
